extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military legal officers, commanders, and others practicing or administering courts-martial/military justice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and precedent-driven rules for construing and applying Articles of War (especially articles 62–73) — what conduct is chargeable, who is subject to military jurisdiction, procedural/authority rules for convening courts-martial, and limits on prosecution. Useful to military lawyers and commanders deciding charges, jurisdiction, and appropriate article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embezzlement under section 5488 (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer who, in his official capacity, receives public money (not pay or an allowance) which he fails duly to account for to the United States, is guilty of embezzlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute makes no distinction as to source of funds or circumstances of receipt; it is immaterial whether the officer actually converted it to his own use or what his motive was. Examples: an officer who exacted moneys from Government contractors and failed to pay into the Treasury or account for them was guilty. See P. 52, 138, Feb. 1892.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returning illegally withdrawn funds is not a defense to embezzlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Restoring funds illegally withdrawn before a formal demand does not constitute a defense to a charge of embezzlement of this class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoration may be shown in mitigation of sentence but does not negate the offense. (R. 25, 588, supra.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between embezzlement under sec. 5488 and 60th article para 9
rubrics_metrics.description: Embezzlement under sec. 5488 is broader and comprehends any public money whether appropriated for military service or other purposes; the 60th article's ninth paragraph concerns money 'furnished for military service' and generally implies felonious conversion with felonious intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where charge overlaps other articles, courts look to statutory definitions and contexts to determine proper article. See Carter v. McClaughry and related opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized payment from public sale proceeds constitutes embezzlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment (e.g., 10% to an enlisted man as compensation for acting as auctioneer) out of proceeds of public sale that is illegal and unauthorized may constitute embezzlement of public money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: payment of auctioneer commission from condemned quartermaster stores proceeds held illegal and chargeable under article. (P. 59, 201, Apr. 1893.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 62 (sixty-second) — breadth and test for application
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 62 covers disorders or neglects to the prejudice of good order and military discipline; whether acts against civilians are within the article depends on circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors supporting cognizability under Article 62: committed on military reservation or premises occupied by the Army or in its neighborhood (constructive presence); committed by an officer or soldier while on duty; injury done to a person the offender was specially required to protect; committed in presence of other soldiers; offender in uniform; use of military position to intimidate or unlawfully influence. Judgment of military officers should be reluctantly disturbed. (R. 49, 268, Aug. 1886; P. 28, 207, Nov. 1888.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sodomy and similar 'bestial' offenses — need for trial rather than summary discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: When soldiers are charged with sodomy and proof is sufficient to warrant a trial, they should be brought to trial by general court-martial rather than summarily discharged without previous trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sufficient evidence to convict is not obtainable, or case is barred by statute of limitations, discharge without honor without trial has been authorized. (C. 20615, Aug. 13, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burglary-like conduct may be charged under Article 62 when pleading omits legal element
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an offense does not satisfy common-law burglary elements (e.g., no breaking), a charge and specification describing forcible nighttime entry with intent to steal may still constitute a disorder to the prejudice of good order and military discipline under Article 62.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will treat the pleading taken together; where essential burglary element is omitted, the conduct may still be sufficiently pleaded as Article 62 disorder. (R. 38, 391, Dec. 1876.)

rubrics_metrics.name: False swearing under Article 62 (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'False swearing' under Article 62, as used in maximum punishment orders, means: (1) taking a false oath in a military judicial proceeding as to a matter not material to the issue; or (2) taking a false oath elsewhere before a person authorized to administer oaths under circumstances affecting interests of the military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such false swearing is an offense under Article 62. (P. 36, 359, Nov. 9, 1889; P. 46, 211, Mar. 1891.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper disposition or sale of issued property — Article 62 (chargeability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper disposition of property in the charge and use of soldiers not covered by article 17 (and similar selling/losing of issued articles) is generally chargeable under Article 62.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items that have been held chargeable under Article 62 rather than Article 17 include sheets, pillows, pillowcases, mattress covers, shelter tents, barrack bags, great-coat straps, tin cups, spoons, knives, forks, meat ration cans, cartridges, etc. (P. 17, 119, May 1887; G. 12796, July 25, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disrespectful language to an officer — Article 62
rubrics_metrics.description: Disrespectful language used regarding a captain by a soldier (even when detached and serving at a hospital) is an offense cognizable by court-martial under Article 62.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: soldier’s insulting remarks to surgeon in charge constituted Article 62 offense. (R. 6, 53, Mar. 1864.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncompliance with NCO orders or offering violence to NCOs — Article 62
rubrics_metrics.description: Noncompliance by a soldier with an order from a noncommissioned officer, or offering violence to the NCO, is in general not an Article 21 offense but should be charged under Article 62.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkenness on duty vs. Article 62 nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: A charge of 'drunkenness on duty' may be unsustained where the accused was drunk at the hour appointed for drill but not at or during the drill; such cases may be more properly charged under Article 62.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court looks to timing and nature of conduct to select proper article. (R. 39, 226, Oct. 1877; C. 15376, Apr. 22, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence from company + drunkenness — proper charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an officer, specially ordered to remain with his company, absents himself and is found drunk while absent, he may not be strictly chargeable under Article 38 but properly under Article 62, disobedience of orders, and unauthorized absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple overlapping charges may be appropriate depending on facts. (R. 38, 425, Jan. 1877.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential authority to set maximum punishments (loaning/usury)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President, as Commander-in-Chief, may prescribe a maximum punishment for the offense of loaning money at usurious rates and may properly make punishment for noncommissioned officers more severe than for privates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 28023, Mar. 27, 1911. This is an administrative/policy determination of comparative punishment authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldiers committing disturbances on private premises while in uniform — Article 62
rubrics_metrics.description: Soldiers who commit a disturbance on private premises while in uniform violate Article 62 as their conduct is prejudicial to good order and military discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence in uniform and resulting effect on discipline are key factors. (C. 16603, July 8, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor delay returning from conditional release may be Article 62
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief delay by an officer permitted to leave confinement temporarily may not properly constitute an offense under the sixty-fifth article, but if sufficiently serious should be charged under Article 62.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charge selection depends on seriousness of delay. (R. 30, 562, Aug. 1870.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to obey order to report in arrest — Article 62 not Article 65
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to obey an order to proceed and report in arrest was held chargeable as an offense under Article 62 and not under Article 65.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar holdings for breaches of arrest not accompanied by confinement to quarters. (R. 31, 606, Aug. 21, 1871; R. 5, 122, Oct. 10, 1863.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated offenses properly chargeable under Article 62 (catalog)
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide range of acts have been held properly charged or chargeable under Article 62 as disorders/neglects prejudicial to good order and military discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included: drunkenness/disorderly conduct when not on duty; escape from confinement (not desertion); breach of arrest (not covered by Article 65); disclosure of court-martial findings contrary to oath; refusal to testify when required; collective letters by inferior officers; neglect by senior officer to assume command; culpable malpractice by medical officer; colluding with bounty brokers; violations of Army Regulations in bidding/purchasing; causing troops to be transported on unsafe vessel; improper payments in contravention of law; inciting duels; impersonating corporals to obtain enlistments; forging orders to procure whisky; breach of faith to post trader; gambling impairing discipline; striking or unnecessary violence by an officer; neglect in overseeing contract execution; public criticism of pending court-martial cases; asserting copyright in official Infantry Drill Regulations; selling condemned stores without proper notice; misconduct at target practice (fraudulent scoring); violating pledge to abstain from intoxicants after condonation; bigamy at military post; disobedience by general prisoner; absence from quarters between inspection and reveille; attempt to commit rape; failure to pay debts when prejudicial to discipline, etc. (Multiple authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts not cognizable under Article 62 (limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain acts have been held not to be cognizable under Article 62 where they are private, remote from post, or do not directly affect military discipline or service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not cognizable examples: mere breach of the peace by a soldier while absent and distant from post in violation of municipal ordinance; pecuniary transactions between enlisted men in private capacity not directly affecting service; speculating/gambling in stocks by a disbursing officer when military duty not affected (though removal from disbursing duty recommended); re-enlisting procured in good faith after disability discharge; resort to civil proceedings against a superior (unless malicious and without probable cause); ordinary loaning at usurious rates by NCOs unless it promoted desertions or seriously demoralized command; becoming infected by vice resulting in unfitness for service (held not cognizable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manslaughter may be included under Article 62
rubrics_metrics.description: The sixty-second article is broad enough to include the offense of manslaughter to the prejudice of good order and military discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple precedents support charging manslaughter under Article 62 where it affects discipline. (R. 11, 592, Mar. 1865; 25, 592, June 1868.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 63 — civilians in quasi-military capacity (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 63 applies principally to civilians serving in a quasi-military capacity in connection with troops during time of war and in the theater of war (teamsters, watchmen, quartermaster department employees, ambulance drivers, telegraph operators, guides, contract surgeons, employees on transports, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application limited to theater and wartime; retainers/camp followers rarely tried by court-martial and are generally dismissed from employment for breaches of discipline. (R. 7, 116, Feb. 1864; R. 23, 331, Nov. 1866.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 63 limits — civilians in time of peace or after war
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilians employed in connection with the Army in time of peace, or civilians employed during Indian wars but not on the theater of such war, cannot be lawfully subjected to Article 63 jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civilians cannot legally be subjected to military jurisdiction under Article 63 after the war during which their offenses were committed has terminated; jurisdiction must be exercised during the status belli. Trials of civilians under Article 63 should be restricted to cases of imperative necessity and ordinary infractions should be handled under civil service regulations. (R. 38, 557, Apr. 1877; R. 38, 641, June 1877; R. 10782, June 29, 1901.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeitures adjudged against civilian employees' pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Forfeitures adjudged by courts-martial against pay of civilian employees under Article 63 should be withheld from their pay and allowed to remain in the appropriation to which the pay pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative handling of forfeitures: C. 9326, Nov. 1900; 10782, June 29, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 65 — unauthorized leaving of confinement (prosecutorial discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although any unauthorized leaving of confinement by an officer is strictly a violation, in view of severe mandatory punishment prescribed, an officer should not, in general, be brought to trial under this article unless his act was of a reckless or deliberately insubordinate character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors/commanders should consider seriousness before convening trial under Article 65. (R. 5, 122, Oct. 1863; 27, 136, Aug. 1868.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regimental commander as 'commanding officer' under Article 65
rubrics_metrics.description: A regimental commander is a 'commanding officer' within the meaning of the sixty-fifth article even though his regiment is part of a higher command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is true even if part of regiment is detached from brigade or post. (C. 26140, Jan. 29, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Release from arrest after placement and trial — Article 65 protection
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer placed in arrest in operation of Article 65 and subsequently tried is not entitled to be released from arrest as a right until the proper reviewing authority has acted on the record of his case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19854, June 24, 1908. Arrest status continues until proper review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 66 — 'crimes' means serious military offenses (confinement policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'crimes' in Article 66 is construed to mean serious military offenses; a soldier should not ordinarily be confined when charged only with a minor offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confinement used for more serious military offenses; see P. 36,78, Oct. 1889; 50, 141, Nov. 1891.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing phrases (Article 71) — 'within ten days thereafter' interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'within ten days thereafter' is held to mean within ten days after his arrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 9, 572, Sept. 1864; C. 15659, Dec. 19, 1903 — clarifies temporal compliance obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of charges — sufficiency despite omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient compliance with requirement as to service of charges may be found where a true copy of charges and specifications is served even though the list of witnesses appended to the original charges was omitted and the charges were not in sufficient legal form and intended to be amended/redrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts allow amendment and view sufficiency in context of intent to proceed. (R. 25, 350, Feb. 1868.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of prolonged arrest at remote posts entitles release
rubrics_metrics.description: Exception for officers put in arrest at remote military posts does not authorize abuse; where arrest was unreasonably protracted without trial, the officer is entitled to be released upon proper application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider communications facilities and circumstances; R. 32, 195, Jan. & Apr. 1872.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to convene general court-martial — attribute of command (Article 72)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority to order a general court-martial under Article 72 is an attribute of command; a department commander absent on leave or separate duty is incompetent during such absence to order a general court-martial and cannot delegate that authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence or being on distinct duty renders the commander incompatible with full legal exercise of the authority; cannot delegate to staff officer or subordinate. (R. 44^, 1880; R. 48, 264, Mar./Apr. 1880; C. 1499, July 1, 1895.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander’s discretionary refusal to convene a court is generally final
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a commander empowered to convene a general court-martial declines, in exercise of his discretion, to approve charges submitted by an inferior and order a court, his decision should generally be regarded as final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 32, 323, Feb. 1872 — deference to command discretion in convening decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corps commander convening courts and limits on confirming severe sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A corps commander may convene a general court-martial under Article 72 and may convene where the division or separate brigade commander is the accuser; however, sound policy requires only the highest military authority to have final power to confirm and execute sentences of death or dismissal unless the corps is a separate and distinct army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory/administrative limits on confirming capital or dismissal sentences; see Secretary of War decisions and multiple citations (R. 11, 543, Mar. 1865; C. 4277, 4710, 5121, 8197, 16710).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assistant adjutant general/staff officers lack authority to relieve/detail members
rubrics_metrics.description: An assistant adjutant general or other staff officer of a department commander is not empowered, of his own authority in the absence of the commander, to relieve an officer duly detailed upon a court-martial or to detail a new officer to the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 43, 332, June 1880 — delegates of commander do not exercise commander’s convening powers by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary command limitations — lieutenant colonel and court appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: A lieutenant colonel in temporary command of a territorial division, department, or army is without authority to appoint a general court-martial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successor unqualified to convene cannot detail members to existing court
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer not qualified under the Article to convene a court-martial cannot issue orders detailing members to a court already appointed, even though he succeeded to the command held by the convening officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 16710, Aug. 25, 1904 — protects limits of convening authority from post hoc expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction follows troops temporarily operating in another department
rubrics_metrics.description: When troops engaged in practice march, joint encampment, or maneuver pass within territorial limits of another department, they pass, for court-martial purposes, from the jurisdiction of their permanent department into that of the commander of the department in which they are temporarily operating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 20052, May 9, 1907 — temporary operational control shifts court-martial jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether convening commander is 'accuser' depends on animus
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the commander who convened the court is to be regarded as the 'accuser or prosecutor' depends largely on his animus in the matter; he may initiate investigation and prefer charges as his act or practically adopt charges due to personal adverse interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-specific inquiry into commander's personal interest and involvement in preparing/preferring charges determines role for conflict/recusal analysis.
